concerns.concern_text: All three acceptance criteria ('customers love the new checkout', 'conversion improves significantly', 'page feels fast') lack any numeric threshold or testable definition. There is no way to objectively determine whether this project has succeeded at release time or in retrospect. Each criterion must be replaced with a specific, measurable target (e.g., 'checkout conversion rate increases by ≥5% vs. baseline measured over 2 weeks post-launch').

The PRD defines no quantitative success metric for the initiative. Without at least one instrumented, measurable KPI with a defined baseline and target, the project cannot be evaluated for success, cannot be used to inform go/no-go decisions post-launch, and cannot support data-driven follow-up prioritization.

The PRD explicitly covers six separate feature areas bundled into a single gate. This increases coordination risk, makes root-cause analysis of post-launch metric changes ambiguous (you won't know which feature drove results), and raises the blast radius of any rollback. Each feature area should be scoped into its own release increment or the bundling must be explicitly justified with a clear sequencing plan.

agent_responses.reasoning: The PRD v2 for Checkout Improvements Q1 has three blocking-level product management issues that prevent design gate approval. First, every acceptance criterion is subjective and unmeasurable — 'love', 'significantly', and 'feels fast' are not testable definitions. No numeric baseline, target, or measurement window is specified for any of them, making it impossible to run a go/no-go evaluation at launch or during review. Second, there is no measurable success metric anywhere in the document; this is a prerequisite for any data-driven product decision. Third, the initiative bundles six distinct feature areas into a single gate, which inflates scope, creates rollback complexity, and makes it impossible to attribute post-launch changes in conversion or performance to any individual feature. The project is blocked until: (1) all acceptance criteria are rewritten with numeric thresholds and measurement windows, (2) at least one primary KPI with baseline and target is added to the PRD, and (3) the multi-feature bundling is either broken into sequenced increments or clearly justified with an explicit sequencing and rollback plan per area.

concerns.concern_text: The PRD describes checkout improvements without any mention of a PCI-DSS scope assessment. Checkout flows inherently touch or transmit cardholder data (PANs, CVVs, billing addresses). No documentation exists confirming whether the service is in-scope for PCI-DSS, whether a SAQ or QSA review is required, or whether card data is fully delegated to a compliant payment processor. This must be resolved before design is approved.

The PRD makes no mention of audit logging for security-sensitive checkout actions such as payment submission, order mutation, address changes, or coupon/discount application. These events must be audit-logged with actor identity and timestamp to meet fraud investigation and compliance requirements.

Checkout flows handle significant PII (names, addresses, email, phone, partial card data). The PRD contains no mention of log redaction controls. Without explicit policy, PII is likely to appear in debug/error logs, violating GDPR and PCI-DSS requirements.

The PRD does not specify encryption-at-rest requirements for any data stores that will hold order records, billing addresses, or other PII/financial data created or modified by the checkout improvements. Encryption posture for new or modified data stores must be documented.

The PRD covers a checkout serving customers across regions but includes no data residency controls or analysis. If EU customer PII (addresses, emails) is replicated to non-EU regions as part of the new checkout data flows, this requires documented GDPR residency controls.

No legal transfer mechanism (SCCs, adequacy decision, etc.) is documented for any cross-border personal data flows that may be introduced or expanded by the checkout improvements. This must be assessed before launch.

agent_responses.reasoning: The PRD for 'Checkout Improvements Q1' describes a broad checkout overhaul but is entirely silent on security and privacy controls. The most critical finding is the absence of any PCI-DSS scope review — checkout improvements by definition touch cardholder data flows, making this a blocking concern. Additional high-severity issues include the lack of audit logging for security-sensitive payment/order actions, no mention of PII log redaction (risking GDPR and PCI-DSS violations in debug logs), and no documented encryption-at-rest posture for new or modified data stores. Medium-severity concerns exist around GDPR data residency for EU customer PII and the absence of any documented cross-border data transfer mechanism. None of these are features or scope questions; they are baseline security and privacy requirements that must be addressed in the design before build begins. I recommend 'approve_with_conditions': the team must (1) complete a PCI-DSS scope assessment and document its outcome, (2) define audit logging requirements for all security-sensitive checkout actions, (3) add explicit log redaction policies, (4) confirm encryption-at-rest for all affected data stores, and (5) document GDPR residency and transfer mechanism analysis before the next gate.
